description: COMSATS Orbit Crew is a health self-check app for astronauts on long missions. It rates NASA's five spaceflight hazards (radiation, isolation, distance, gravity and closed environment) as Good, Watch or Act now, and tells the astronaut what to do today. It works offline, because help from Earth can be 20+ minutes away. I'm a CS student at COMSATS Islamabad and I build AI and data apps with Python. Happy to team up with someone into data visualization or design.
summary: In spaceflight, "nominal" means everything is going to plan. NOMINAL is a daily health self-check that helps astronauts on long missions stay that way. Every morning the astronaut gathers their health indicators in a 2-minute check-in: sleep, mood, stress, blood pressure, heart rate, body temperature, blood sugar, exercise and a built-in reaction-time test, plus onboard readings for radiation dose and cabin CO2. NOMINAL then evaluates each reading against the astronaut's own start-of-mission baseline and NASA limits, and rates NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight as nominal, caution or warning. When something needs attention, it guides the astronaut to act with step-by-step onboard procedures. It works fully offline, because on the way to Mars a message to Earth takes up to 22 minutes each way, so the crew has to spot and handle problems themselves.
details:
What it does

NOMINAL follows the three verbs in the challenge: gather, evaluate and act.

- Gather: a 7-step check-in with one question per screen and large controls for a tired astronaut in a dim cabin. It covers sleep, mood, stress, symptoms, blood pressure, heart rate, body temperature, fasting blood sugar, exercise, and a 30-second reaction-time test modeled on the psychomotor vigilance test that NASA uses in its Reaction Self Test on the ISS. Every measurement has a plain "How to measure" and "Why it matters in space" explanation, so the astronaut never has to guess.

- Evaluate: a status screen rates each of NASA's five hazards (radiation, isolation, distance, gravity and closed environment) as nominal, caution or warning. Each reading is compared with the astronaut's own baseline from the first 14 days of the mission, and with NASA limits such as the 600 mSv career radiation limit. Every finding is a plain sentence with real numbers, for example "Reaction time is 16% slower than your baseline (293 ms vs 252 ms)."

- Body view: a clickable human figure. Each body system shows its status, the exact NASA Human Research Program risk it relates to, what spaceflight does to it, the astronaut's readings and how to check it.

- Act: 7 onboard procedures (sleep recovery, fatigue no-go for critical tasks, low mood support, CO2 symptom response, solar storm shelter, vision change check for SANS, exercise catch-up) written as numbered checklists, the format astronauts already use.

- Trends: charts of every indicator against the personal baseline band, with mission events marked.

- Downlink: a ready report for Mission Control, queued for the next contact window with the signal delay shown.

- Mission profiles: Mars transit, Mars surface base and ISS, each with its own radiation rate, gravity and signal delay.

- Routine: a daily list of due measurements and a check-in streak, so health checks become part of the mission day.

How it works

All evaluation runs on the device, with no internet and no server. Rules compare the last 7 days with the personal baseline and with NASA limits. Colors follow spacecraft caution and warning practice: red only for warning, amber only for caution, green for nominal, and every status also has an icon and a word. The demo astronaut and sensor history are simulated, and the app says so. Rates and limits come from NASA sources.

Benefits

- Catches slow changes like sleep debt, fatigue or CO2 headaches before they become emergencies.

- Gives clear next steps instead of raw numbers.

- Works anywhere, at any distance from Earth.

Tools

React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Lucide icons, IBM Plex fonts, hand-built SVG charts and body figure. Hosted on Vercel. Code on GitHub: https://github.com/asimsaeed681/nominal

Future work

Connect real wearable sensors, add a crew medical officer view for the whole crew, and have flight surgeons tune the thresholds.
